back: A wrapper around calls to one dependency that stops calling it when it is failing, so callers fail fast and the dependency can recover.
Closed: healthy, calls flow and outcomes are recorded. Open: calls are blocked and fail fast. Same as an electrical circuit.
After the open wait, a few trial calls are let through. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it for another wait.
Closing straight to full traffic can knock over a recovering (e.g. cold-cache) service again, making the breaker flap.
Retry outside the breaker so each attempt is recorded. Never retry a breaker-open rejection (Resilience4j: CallNotPermittedException).
Timeouts, 5xx, refused connections. Not 4xx client errors: one buggy caller should not cut everyone off.
50% failure-rate threshold, a count-based window of the last 100 calls, 60 s wait in the open state.

front: Why a minimum number of calls?
back: So a low-traffic breaker doesn't trip on 1 failure out of 2 calls. The rate is only evaluated once enough calls are in the window.
At high traffic a 1% error rate occasionally produces N failures in a row; at low traffic a dead service takes ages to reach N.

front: What limits how fast a breaker trips?
back: The timeout. A hanging call records no outcome until it times out, so a 30 s timeout means no failures recorded for 30 s.
Per-host health tracking that ejects one bad replica from the pool (Envoy: after consecutive 5xx, 5 by default), leaving healthy replicas in use.
Concurrency limits per upstream cluster: max connections, pending requests, requests and retries. Overload protection, not a failure-rate state machine.
Reject locally with probability max(0, (requests − K × accepts) / (requests + 1)), K ≈ 2, over the last two minutes. A smooth alternative to on/off.
Cached or stale value, generic default, degraded response, accept and defer via a queue, or fail fast with a clear error.

front: When is failing fast the right fallback?
back: When any guess is harmful: payments, permissions, prices beyond a staleness bound, and most writes.

front: How can a fallback hide an outage?
back: It keeps user-facing errors low, so nothing alerts. Alert on breaker state (e.g. open > 5 min) and fallback rate.
Netflix put it in maintenance mode in 2018 and pointed users to Resilience4j. .NET teams commonly use Polly.
